## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ekapaṇṇajātaka* (Ja 149), titled *One Poison Leaf* in English, is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to its commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Great Forest near Vesālī, occasioned by a fierce or wicked Licchavi prince (*duṭṭha-Licchavikumāra*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The verse begins with the opening words *Ekapanno ayam rukkho* [Fausböll 1877]. In the narrative of the past, a wise ascetic guides a young prince to uproot a poisonous sapling before it can mature and cause widespread harm, illustrating practical foresight and wisdom regarding future consequences rather than an absence of compassion [UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. In the identification of characters (*samodhāna*), the wicked prince is identified with the Licchavi youth, the king with Ānanda, and the wise advising ascetic (*ovādadāyakatāpasa*) with the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1877].

Neither curated parallels on SuttaCentral nor automated text-reuse matches on DharmaNexus are reported for this Jātaka within the Pali canon or across external Buddhist corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations of the tale across four languages [SuttaCentral]. The canonical verse and its accompanying commentary were edited by V. Fausböll in the first volume of his critical edition of the *Jātaka* [Fausböll 1877].
